newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: MANILA SAYS ASEAN ECONOMIES MUST GROW.
newsitem.headline: MANILA SAYS ASEAN ECONOMIES MUST GROW.

text.p: Southeast Asia's defeated rebel groups could spring back to life if the region's economies fail to keep up with the rest of the world, Philippine Foreign Secretary Domingo Siazon said.

Siazon, speaking to Philippine ambassadors on Wednesday, said members of the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) must produce concrete benefits to convince their peoples that the decision to liberalise their economies was good for them.
The speech was released by his office on Thursday.
Siazon said the region's economic growth had helped defeat the leftist insurgencies challenging the legitimacy of ASEAN governments.
"(But) questions of legitimacy may again resurface" in the region's transition to a globalised economy, he said.
He said globalisation had led to rapid change, including intense urbanisation and a new, articulate middle class.
"All of this will strain the traditional social fabric in the region, unsettle all political systems, whether these be communist or right-wing, authoritarian or liberal democratic."
"You cannot open the eyes of the people and expect them not to see and compare their countries with other countries. That is part of the baggage...of globalisation," Siazon said.
He said ASEAN must make itself relevant to the lives of people lest it be perceived as nothing more than "a country club of the established order" that had reached a dead-end.
"Our duty...is to lay the groundwork today, so that ASEAN does not go the way of the dinosaur," he said.
ASEAN groups Brunei, Burma, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam. Cambodia is still an observer.
